task_description: I need to email my team asking for architecture review on a new caching layer proposal — I only want feedback on the invalidation strategy, not the implementation details yet.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Writes emails that eliminate the need for follow-up meetings. Every email provides enough context for the reader to understand, decide, and act asynchronously. Values decision transparency and thread hygiene.

rubric.name: Decision Tradeoff Transparency
rubric.description: Emails about decisions include the options that were considered and why the chosen path was selected. Stating a decision without alternatives is an edict, not communication.

dimensions.label: Names at least one alternative that was seriously considered
Explains why each alternative was rejected with specific reasoning, not just 'it didn't fit'
Acknowledges what the chosen option sacrifices compared to alternatives
The decision itself appears in the first two sentences, not after paragraphs of context

rubric.name: Link, Don't Duplicate
rubric.description: Links to existing documents, PRs, dashboards, or design docs replace inline explanations. If information exists somewhere canonical, the email links to it rather than creating a duplicate that will drift.

dimensions.label: References to existing docs, PRs, or dashboards are hyperlinked, not described in prose
Does not reproduce information that's already available at a linked source
Each link has enough surrounding context that the reader knows why to click it

rubric.name: Scoped Review Requests
rubric.description: Review requests specify what kind of feedback is needed and by when. 'Please review' without scope or deadline gets deprioritized — the request must tell the reader exactly what to focus on.

dimensions.label: Specifies the type of feedback requested (architecture, implementation, naming, security, etc.)
Includes a specific deadline or timeframe for the review
Explicitly notes what is NOT in scope for this review round

rubric.name: Thread Discipline
rubric.description: One topic per email thread. If the conversation drifts to a new topic, a new thread with a new subject line is started. Never continues a thread whose subject no longer matches the content.

dimensions.label: The email addresses exactly one topic — does not bundle unrelated items
The subject line accurately describes the current content, not a prior topic in the thread
When introducing a new topic, starts a fresh thread rather than replying to an existing one

rubric_used.coaching_notes: Rachel's philosophy: if someone needs a meeting after reading your email, the email failed. Non-negotiable: decisions always include what was rejected and why. Will push back hard on unbounded review requests or emails that cover multiple topics in one thread.

rounds.draft:
Subject: Architecture Review Request: Caching Layer Invalidation Strategy (feedback by [DATE])

---

Hi team,

We're moving forward with adding a dedicated caching layer to [system/service name]. I'd like your architecture review on the invalidation strategy specifically — details below.

**The proposal:** [link to design doc]

**What I'm asking you to review:**
The invalidation strategy section only (section X.X in the doc). Specifically, I want to know whether the approach is sound at the architecture level — correctness under concurrent writes, failure modes, and consistency guarantees.

**What's out of scope for this round:**
Implementation details, library choices, and cache warming logic are not up for review yet. Please hold that feedback for a follow-up pass once the invalidation strategy is settled.

**Please submit feedback by [DATE/TIME + timezone]** as comments in the doc or as a reply to this thread.

---

For context on why we landed on this approach: we chose **[chosen strategy, e.g., event-driven invalidation]** over two alternatives we seriously considered:

- **[Alternative A, e.g., TTL-based expiration]** — rejected because [specific reason, e.g., our write patterns are too unpredictable for TTL windows to reliably prevent stale reads without setting TTLs so short they eliminate cache benefit].
- **[Alternative B, e.g., write-through invalidation]** — rejected because [specific reason, e.g., it would require synchronous cache writes on every DB update, which adds latency we can't absorb on the critical path].

The tradeoff we're accepting with event-driven invalidation is [e.g., added operational complexity — we're now dependent on the reliability of the event bus, and cache inconsistency windows widen if events are delayed]. That felt like the right call given [brief rationale], but it's worth flagging if you see that differently.

Thanks,
[Your name]
